title: totalme
text: In a model with several outcome categories – a multinomial or ordered logit, or the probabilities of individual counts – a predictor has one marginal effect per category. totalme summarizes them in a single Total Marginal Effect: the total amount of probability the predictor moves across the outcome categories, with a standard error. The summary can be reported for one model, compared across predictors, and compared across models or groups.

title: totalme
text:
Installation
net install totalme, from("https://tdmize.github.io/data/totalme") replace

title: totalme
text:
Basic use

sysuse nlsw88, clear
(NLSW, 1988 extract)
drop if missing(occupation)
(9 observations deleted)
recode occupation (1/2 = 1 "Professional/managerial") (3/5 = 2 "Sales/clerical/craft") ///
                  (6/13 = 3 "Other"), gen(occ3)
(1,920 differences between occupation and occ3)

. 
quietly mlogit occ3 i.collgrad c.age i.south, vce(robust)
. 
totalme collgrad
Model (totalme_mod1) is:
     mlogit occ3 i.collgrad c.age i.south, vce(robust)
Continuous/Binary IV(s): 
     collgrad

Total ME Estimates (N = 2237)

                         |   Estimate   Std. err.           z       P>|z| 
-------------------------+-----------------------------------------------
collgrad                 |                                               
College grad vs Not co~d |      0.245       0.021      11.474       0.000 

The Total Marginal Effect of a college degree is the total change in the predicted distribution across the three occupation groups. totalme can also be requested as an option of mecompare, which places the summary beneath the per-outcome marginal effects.

help totalme in Stata documents the syntax and options.

title: metest
text: metest tests linear and nonlinear combinations of the rows of the table produced by mecompare, meinequality, or totalme – or of any results posted by margins, post. Rows are referred to by the number in the # column of the table, so a difference between two effects is metest 2 - 1, a ratio is metest 2 / 1, and a test that several effects are equal is metest 1 = 2 = 3.

title: metest
text:
Installation
net install metest, from("https://tdmize.github.io/data/metest") replace

title: metest
text:
Basic use

sysuse nlsw88, clear
(NLSW, 1988 extract)
drop if missing(union)
(368 observations deleted)

. 
quietly logit union i.collgrad i.south i.smsa c.age c.wage, vce(robust)
estimates store m
. 
mecompare i.collgrad i.south i.smsa, models(m)
Predicting: Pr(union)

Marginal effects (N_m=1878)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
collgrad                         |                                       
         College  - Not coll     |                                       
                               m |     1      0.056      0.025      0.026
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
south                            |                                       
            South - Not sout     |                                       
                               m |     2     -0.114      0.020      0.000
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
smsa                             |                                       
             SMSA - Not SMSA     |                                       
                               m |     3      0.031      0.022      0.161

Is the college gap in union membership the same size as the regional gap? And is the college gap larger than the city/non-city gap?

metest 1 - 2
                                 |  estimate         se     pvalue 
---------------------------------+--------------------------------
                collgrad - south |     0.170      0.034      0.000 
metest 1 - 3
                                 |  estimate         se     pvalue 
---------------------------------+--------------------------------
                 collgrad - smsa |     0.025      0.034      0.465

title: metest
text:
Documentation
help metest in Stata documents the syntax, the forms an expression can take, and the options for accumulating several tests into one table.

title: mecompare
text:
mecompare calculates marginal effects and compares them across models. It fits the framework of Mize, Doan, and Long (2019): the models are combined with suest2 so that the difference between a marginal effect in one model and the same effect in another has a proper standard error, even though the models were estimated separately.
The comparisons it handles include effects across nested models (mediation and confounding), across alternative predictors, across different outcomes, across different model types (for example ordinal versus nominal), and across models fit to separate groups or samples. It also compares effects within a single model.

title: mecompare
text:
Installation
net install mecompare, from("https://tdmize.github.io/data/mecompare") replace
mecompare calls suest2 and works with metest, which tests contrasts between rows of the mecompare table. Each installs the same way.

title: mecompare
text:
Where to start

Getting started walks through one comparison and explains the table.
The Examples in the sidebar reproduce the examples from Section 6 of Mize, Doan, and Long (2019) plus a within-model comparison.
The help file (help mecompare in Stata) documents every option.

title: mecompare
text:
Citation
If you use mecompare, please cite:

Mize, Trenton D., Long Doan, and J. Scott Long. 2019. “A General Framework for Comparing Predictions and Marginal Effects Across Models.” Sociological Methodology 49(1): 152–189. https://doi.org/10.1177/0081175019852763

title: mecompare
text:
Related commands




Command
What it does




suest2
Combines separately estimated models so that quantities from different models can be tested against each other. The engine underneath mecompare.


metest
Tests contrasts between rows of the tables produced by mecompare, meinequality, and totalme (or any posted margins results).


meinequality
Summarizes how unequal the marginal effects of a categorical predictor are across its categories.


totalme
Summarizes a predictor’s effect across all outcome categories of a multiple-outcome model in a single Total Marginal Effect.

title: Within a single model
text:
The primary purpose of mecompare is to compare effects across models, but with one model in models() it reports the marginal effects of the listed variables and metest compares them. Here: does a college degree or being married have the larger association with being very happy?

use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss_cme", clear
(gss_cme.dta | GSS 1972 - 2016 Weighted | 2018-07-10)
drop if year < 2000
(38,116 observations deleted)
drop if employed != 1
(9,556 observations deleted)
drop if missing(vhappy, college, wages, occprest, age, married, parent, woman, conserv, reltrad)
(5,578 observations deleted)

. 
quietly logit vhappy i.college i.married i.parent i.woman i.conserv i.race i.reltrad ///
              i.year c.age##c.age c.occprest, vce(robust)
estimates store happymod


mecompare i.college i.married, models(happymod)
Predicting: Pr(vhappy)

Marginal effects (N_happymod=9216)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
college                          |                                       
         College  - No Col D     |                                       
                        happymod |     1      0.033      0.012      0.004
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
married                          |                                       
          Married - Not Marr     |                                       
                        happymod |     2      0.200      0.010      0.000

metest takes an expression in the row numbers from the # column. The difference between the two marginal effects, with its standard error:

metest 2 - 1
                                 |  estimate         se     pvalue 
---------------------------------+--------------------------------
               married - college |     0.167      0.016      0.000 

Any linear or nonlinear combination of rows works the same way – for example a ratio, metest 2 / 1, or a test that several effects are equal, metest 1 = 2.



 Back to top

title: Different model types
text:
Marginal effects are on the scale of the outcome – here, probabilities of each party-identification category – so they can be compared across models that make different assumptions about the outcome. This example fits an ordered logit and a multinomial logit to the same five-category party identification variable with the same predictors, and asks whether the two models imply different effects of age.

use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss_cme", clear
(gss_cme.dta | GSS 1972 - 2016 Weighted | 2018-07-10)
drop if year < 2010
(53,043 observations deleted)
drop if missing(partyid5, woman, edyrs, age, parent, married, faminc, employed, region4, year)
(1,244 observations deleted)

. 
quietly ologit partyid5 c.age##c.age i.woman c.edyrs i.parent i.married i.race ///
               c.faminc i.employed i.region4 i.year, vce(robust)
estimates store ordinal
. 
quietly mlogit partyid5 c.age##c.age i.woman c.edyrs i.parent i.married i.race ///
               c.faminc i.employed i.region4 i.year, vce(robust)
estimates store nominal

Age enters with a squared term, so the marginal effect depends on where the change starts. start(age=20) and amount(10) define the effect as the change in each probability from age 20 to age 30, with the other variables held at their means:

mecompare age, models(ordinal nominal) start(age=20) amount(10) covariates(atmeans)
Model 1 (ordinal) is:
     ologit partyid5 c.age##c.age i.woman c.edyrs i.parent i.married i.race c.faminc i.employed i.re
> gion4 i.year
Model 2 (nominal) is:
     mlogit partyid5 c.age##c.age i.woman c.edyrs i.parent i.married i.race c.faminc i.employed i.re
> gion4 i.year


Predicting: Pr(partyid5==0) (ordinal), Pr(partyid5==1) (nominal)

Marginal effects and cross-model differences (N_ordinal=8179) (N_nominal=8179)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
age + 10                         |                                       
            Strong Dem - ordinal |     1      0.021      0.004      0.000
            Strong Dem - nominal |     2      0.029      0.003      0.000
         Strong Dem - Difference |     3     -0.008      0.003      0.011
              Democrat - ordinal |     4      0.028      0.007      0.000
              Democrat - nominal |     5     -0.008      0.013      0.556
           Democrat - Difference |     6      0.035      0.011      0.001
           Independent - ordinal |     7     -0.002      0.001      0.033
           Independent - nominal |     8      0.008      0.012      0.485
        Independent - Difference |     9     -0.010      0.012      0.400
            Republican - ordinal |    10     -0.028      0.006      0.000
            Republican - nominal |    11     -0.039      0.013      0.004
         Republican - Difference |    12      0.011      0.012      0.346
          Strong Repub - ordinal |    13     -0.020      0.005      0.000
          Strong Repub - nominal |    14      0.009      0.003      0.005
       Strong Repub - Difference |    15     -0.029      0.005      0.000

Each outcome category gets its own block of the table. Where the Difference rows are large relative to their standard errors, the ordinal model’s proportional-odds assumption is changing the substantive conclusion for that category.

title: Separate samples or groups
text:
When a model is fit separately to two groups – here, GSS respondents in 1986 and in 2016 – the question is whether an effect differs between the groups. mecompare with the groups option compares marginal effects across models that were estimated on non-overlapping samples. The example asks whether the association between political conservatism and support for government help with medical costs changed over 30 years.

use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss_cme", clear
(gss_cme.dta | GSS 1972 - 2016 Weighted | 2018-07-10)
drop if missing(helpsickB, polviews, faminc, employed, woman, age, college, married, parent)
(36,143 observations deleted)

. 
quietly logit helpsickB i.conserv faminc i.employed i.woman age i.college i.married i.parent i.rac
e ///
              if year == 1986, vce(robust)
estimates store mod1986
. 
quietly logit helpsickB i.conserv faminc i.employed i.woman age i.college i.married i.parent i.rac
e ///
              if year == 2016, vce(robust)
estimates store mod2016


mecompare i.conserv, models(mod1986 mod2016) groups
Model 1 (mod1986) is:
     logit helpsickB i.conserv faminc i.employed i.woman age i.college i.married i.parent i.race
Model 2 (mod2016) is:
     logit helpsickB i.conserv faminc i.employed i.woman age i.college i.married i.parent i.race


Predicting: Pr(helpsickB)

Marginal effects and cross-model differences (N_mod1986=1254) (N_mod2016=1670)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
conserv                          |                                       
         Conserva - Not Cons     |                                       
                         mod1986 |     1     -0.092      0.030      0.002
                         mod2016 |     2     -0.258      0.025      0.000
                      Difference |     3      0.166      0.039      0.000

groups tells mecompare that each model’s estimation sample is a different group, so the marginal effect for each model is averaged over that model’s own sample. The Difference row tests whether the conservatism gap in 2016 differs from the gap in 1986.




 Back to top

title: Alternative predictors
text:
Two models can differ in how the same construct is measured. Here support for same-sex relationships is predicted by sexual orientation measured two ways: by reported sexual behavior in one model and by self-identification in the other. mecompare puts the marginal effects of both measures in one table and allows a test of whether the measures give the same answer.

use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss_cme", clear
(gss_cme.dta | GSS 1972 - 2016 Weighted | 2018-07-10)
drop if missing(samesexB, sexident, sexbehav, college, woman, race, age, year)
(57,545 observations deleted)

. 
quietly logit samesexB i.sexbehav i.woman i.college c.age i.race i.year, vce(robust)
estimates store behavior
. 
quietly logit samesexB i.sexident i.woman i.college c.age i.race i.year, vce(robust)
estimates store identity

Each predictor appears in only one of the models, so the table reports each effect for the model that contains it:

mecompare i.sexbehav i.sexident, models(behavior identity)
Model 1 (behavior) is:
     logit samesexB i.sexbehav i.woman i.college c.age i.race i.year
Model 2 (identity) is:
     logit samesexB i.sexident i.woman i.college c.age i.race i.year


Predicting: Pr(samesexB)

Marginal effects and cross-model differences (N_behavior=4921) (N_identity=4921)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
sexbehav                         |                                       
       Bisexual - Heterosexu     |                                       
                        behavior |     1     -0.097      0.023      0.000
                        identity |                                       
                      Difference |                                       
            Gay - Heterosexu     |                                       
                        behavior |     2     -0.362      0.038      0.000
                        identity |                                       
                      Difference |                                       
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
sexident                         |                                       
       Bisexual - Heterosexu     |                                       
                        behavior |                                       
                        identity |     3     -0.274      0.041      0.000
                      Difference |                                       
            Gay - Heterosexu     |                                       
                        behavior |                                       
                        identity |     4     -0.428      0.034      0.000
                      Difference |                                       

Contrasts across the two measures – for example, whether the bisexual versus heterosexual difference is the same when measured by behavior as when measured by identity – are contrasts between rows of this table. Use metest with the row numbers from the # column, as in the within-model example.

title: Stata software
text:
Documentation for the Stata commands written by Trenton D. Mize. Each command has its own set of pages; installation instructions are on each overview page.




Command
What it does




mecompare
Marginal effects, and tests of whether an effect differs across models: nested models, alternative predictors, different outcomes, different model types, separate groups.


suest2
Combines separately estimated models so that quantities from different models can be tested against each other.


metest
Tests contrasts between rows of the tables produced by mecompare, meinequality, and totalme.


meinequality
Summarizes how unequal the marginal effects of a categorical predictor are across its categories.


totalme
Summarizes a predictor’s effect across all outcome categories of a multiple-outcome model in a single Total Marginal Effect.




Other software – the cleanplots graph scheme, irt_me, and R packages – is listed at trentonmize.com/software.

title: Different outcomes
text:
The same predictors can have different effects on different outcomes. Here two negative binomial models predict days of poor mental health and days of poor physical health from the same set of variables, and mecompare tests whether each predictor matters more for one outcome than the other. With no variable listed before the comma, marginal effects are computed for every predictor in the models.

use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss_cme", clear
(gss_cme.dta | GSS 1972 - 2016 Weighted | 2018-07-10)
drop if missing(mntlhlth, physhlth, woman, married, age, faminc, race, college, parent, reltrad)
(57,404 observations deleted)

. 
quietly nbreg mntlhlth i.woman i.married i.parent i.college c.age faminc i.race i.year, vce(robust
)
estimates store mental
. 
quietly nbreg physhlth i.woman i.married i.parent i.college c.age faminc i.race i.year, vce(robust
)
estimates store physical

For the count models the marginal effects are changes in the predicted rate (expected number of days). Continuous predictors are changed by one standard deviation:

mecompare, models(mental physical) amount(sd)
Model 1 (mental) is:
     nbreg mntlhlth i.woman i.married i.parent i.college c.age faminc i.race i.year
Model 2 (physical) is:
     nbreg physhlth i.woman i.married i.parent i.college c.age faminc i.race i.year


Predicting: Predicted mean of mntlhlth (mental), Predicted mean of physhlth (physical)

title: Curvilinear effects and mediation
text:
Marginal effects summarize a curvilinear relationship in a single number, and comparing that number across a model with and without a proposed mediator tests how much of the effect the mediator accounts for. Here income is entered with a squared term in a linear regression of depressive symptoms; the second model adds job satisfaction as a mediator.

use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/ah4_cme", clear
(ah4_cme.dta | Add Health Wave 4 | 2018-07-10)
drop if missing(depsympB, income, inc10, age, woman, race, college, jobsat)
(0 observations deleted)

. 
quietly regress depsympB c.income##c.income c.age i.woman i.race, vce(robust)
estimates store basemod
. 
quietly regress depsympB c.income##c.income c.age i.woman i.race i.jobsat, vce(robust)
estimates store medmod

The marginal effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in income in each model, and the difference between them:

mecompare income, models(basemod medmod) amount(sd)
Model 1 (basemod) is:
     regress depsympB c.income##c.income c.age i.woman i.race
Model 2 (medmod) is:
     regress depsympB c.income##c.income c.age i.woman i.race i.jobsat


Predicting: Linear prediction

Marginal effects and cross-model differences (N_basemod=4307) (N_medmod=4307)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
income + SD                      |                                       
                         basemod |     1     -0.982      0.098      0.000
                          medmod |     2     -0.797      0.096      0.000
                      Difference |     3     -0.184      0.027      0.000

The Difference row is the part of the income effect that runs through job satisfaction, with a standard error that accounts for the two models being estimated on the same data. The proportion of the effect that is mediated is a contrast between rows, so metest can report it with a standard error:

metest (1 - 2) / 1
                                 |  estimate         se     pvalue 
---------------------------------+--------------------------------
income                           |                                
    (basemod - medmod) / basemod |     0.188      0.030      0.000 




 Back to top

title: Nested logit models
text:
The most common cross-model question is whether an effect changes when controls are added. Here the effect of a college degree on the probability of being very happy is compared between a bivariate logit and a logit with a full set of controls. Because the outcome is binary, the marginal effect is a discrete change in the predicted probability, and comparing it across models is not subject to the rescaling problem that makes comparing logit coefficients across models misleading.

use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss_cme", clear
(gss_cme.dta | GSS 1972 - 2016 Weighted | 2018-07-10)
drop if year < 2000
(38,116 observations deleted)
drop if employed != 1
(9,556 observations deleted)
drop if missing(vhappy, college, wages, occprest, age, married, parent, woman, conserv, reltrad)
(5,578 observations deleted)

. 
quietly logit vhappy i.college, vce(robust)
estimates store mod1
. 
quietly logit vhappy i.college i.married i.parent i.woman i.conserv ///
              i.reltrad i.year c.age##c.age, vce(robust)
estimates store mod2


mecompare i.college, models(mod1 mod2)
Model 1 (mod1) is:
     logit vhappy i.college
Model 2 (mod2) is:
     logit vhappy i.college i.married i.parent i.woman i.conserv i.reltrad i.year c.age##c.age


Predicting: Pr(vhappy)

Marginal effects and cross-model differences (N_mod1=9216) (N_mod2=9216)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
college                          |                                       
         College  - No Col D     |                                       
                            mod1 |     1      0.072      0.010      0.000
                            mod2 |     2      0.060      0.011      0.000
                      Difference |     3      0.012      0.004      0.003

The Difference row tests whether the college effect is smaller once the controls are included. More than two nested models can be compared by running mecompare for each pair of interest.



 Back to top

title: Getting started
text: Every mecompare analysis has the same three steps: fit the models, store them, compare. This page runs through one example with Stata’s nlsw88 data and then explains how to read the table.

title: Getting started
text:
1. Fit and store the models
The question: does the association between having a college degree and union membership change once we account for wages and work experience? Fit the model without those variables, then the model with them, storing each with estimates store.

sysuse nlsw88, clear
(NLSW, 1988 extract)
drop if missing(union)
(368 observations deleted)

. 
quietly logit union i.collgrad c.age i.south i.smsa, vce(robust)
estimates store base
. 
quietly logit union i.collgrad c.age i.south i.smsa c.wage c.ttl_exp, vce(robust)
estimates store full

Nothing here is specific to mecompare; any estimation command that works with margins can be used, and vce(robust) is recommended because the models will be combined with suest2.

title: Getting started
text:
2. Compare the marginal effects
Name the variable whose effect you want and the stored models in models().

mecompare i.collgrad, models(base full)
Model 1 (base) is:
     logit union i.collgrad c.age i.south i.smsa
Model 2 (full) is:
     logit union i.collgrad c.age i.south i.smsa c.wage c.ttl_exp


Predicting: Pr(union)

Marginal effects and cross-model differences (N_base=1878) (N_full=1878)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
collgrad                         |                                       
         College  - Not coll     |                                       
                            base |     1      0.092      0.024      0.000
                            full |     2      0.057      0.025      0.024
                      Difference |     3      0.035      0.009      0.000

title: Getting started
text:
3. Read the table
Each block of the table is one marginal effect. For a binary or factor variable the effect is the discrete change in the predicted probability between its levels; for a continuous variable it is the change for a one-unit increase (other amounts are set with amount()). Within a block:

the first rows give the marginal effect in each model, in the order the models were listed in models();
the Difference row is the effect in the first model minus the effect in the second, with a standard error and p-value that account for the fact that both effects were estimated from the same data.

The # column numbers the rows so that you can refer to them in metest for any other contrast.

title: Getting started
section: Continuous variables and the size of the change
text:
Continuous variables and the size of the change
For a continuous variable, amount() sets the size of the change. Here the effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in age:

mecompare age, models(base full) amount(sd)
Model 1 (base) is:

title: Getting started
text:
Comparing effects within one model
With a single model in models(), mecompare reports the marginal effects of the variables listed, and metest compares them. Here, is the union-membership gap by college degree the same size as the gap by region?

mecompare i.collgrad i.south, models(full)
Predicting: Pr(union)

Marginal effects (N_full=1878)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
collgrad                         |                                       
         College  - Not coll     |                                       
                            full |     1      0.057      0.025      0.024
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
south                            |                                       
            South - Not sout     |                                       
                            full |     2     -0.114      0.020      0.000
metest 1 - 2
                                 |  estimate         se     pvalue 
---------------------------------+--------------------------------
                collgrad - south |     0.171      0.034      0.000

title: Getting started
text:
Frequently used options
The help file (help mecompare) documents everything; these are the options that come up most often.



Option
Purpose




models(name1 [name2])
The stored estimates to compare. One model gives marginal effects for that model alone.


amount()
Size of the change for a continuous variable: a number, sd or 2sd (one or two standard deviations), or rate (the instantaneous rate of change).


start()
Where the change in a continuous variable begins: start(varname=#) or start(atmeans).


covariates(varname=# ...), atmeans
Hold other variables at specified values or at their means (the default averages over the observed values).


by(varlist)
Marginal effects within each level of another variable, in one table, so that they can be compared with metest.


over(varlist)
Marginal effects within subsamples defined by another variable.


pwcompare
All pairwise contrasts among the levels of a nominal variable, not just contrasts with the base level.


groups
The models were fit to separate groups (see the groups example).


totalme, meinequality
Add the Total Marginal Effect or the marginal-effect inequality summary for the compared effects.


store(stub)
Store the results so that they can be graphed with coefplot or tabled with esttab.

title: meinequality
text: A nominal predictor with several categories produces a set of marginal effects – one contrast for every pair of categories. meinequality summarizes that set in a single measure of how unequal the categories are, with a standard error, so that the overall importance of a categorical variable can be reported, compared across predictors, and compared across models or groups.

title: meinequality
text:
Installation
net install meinequality, from("https://tdmize.github.io/data/meinequality") replace

title: meinequality
text:
Basic use

sysuse nlsw88, clear
(NLSW, 1988 extract)
drop if missing(union)
(368 observations deleted)

. 
quietly logit union i.race i.collgrad c.age i.south, vce(robust)
. 
meinequality race
Model (meineq_mod1) is:
     logit union i.race i.collgrad c.age i.south, vce(robust)

ME Inequality Estimates (N = 1878)

                         |   Estimate   Std. err.           z       P>|z| 
-------------------------+-----------------------------------------------
ME Inequality            |                                               
                    race |      0.106       0.025       4.225       0.000 

With no models() option the summary is computed for the model in memory; with two stored models in models() it is computed for each and the difference is tested, as in mecompare.

title: meinequality
text: Citation

title: meinequality
text:
Documentation
help meinequality in Stata documents the syntax and options. The same summary is available as an option of mecompare, which places it beneath the marginal effects it summarizes.

title: suest2
text: suest2 combines models that were estimated separately into one set of results, so that coefficients, predictions, and marginal effects from different models can be tested against each other with test, lincom, nlcom, or margins. It is the engine underneath mecompare, meinequality, and totalme, and it can be used on its own.

title: suest2
text:
Installation
net install suest2, from("https://tdmize.github.io/data/suest2") replace

title: suest2
text:
Basic use
Fit and store the models, then combine them and refer to each model’s coefficients by equation name:

sysuse nlsw88, clear
(NLSW, 1988 extract)
drop if missing(union)
(368 observations deleted)

. 
quietly logit union i.collgrad c.age i.south, vce(robust)
estimates store m1
. 
quietly logit union i.collgrad c.age i.south c.wage c.ttl_exp, vce(robust)
estimates store m2
. 
suest2 m1 m2
Simultaneous results for m1, m2                          Number of obs = 1,878

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
              |               Robust
              | Coefficient  std. err.      z    P>|z|     [95% conf. interval]
--------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
m1_union      |
     collgrad |
College grad  |      0.507      0.119    4.246   0.000        0.273       0.741
          age |      0.009      0.018    0.519   0.604       -0.026       0.044
              |
        south |
       South  |     -0.747      0.116   -6.431   0.000       -0.974      -0.519
        _cons |     -1.340      0.704   -1.903   0.057       -2.720       0.040
--------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
m2_union      |
     collgrad |
College grad  |      0.311      0.132    2.356   0.018        0.052       0.570
          age |      0.008      0.018    0.428   0.668       -0.028       0.043
              |
        south |
       South  |     -0.677      0.118   -5.719   0.000       -0.909      -0.445
         wage |      0.054      0.014    3.820   0.000        0.026       0.081
      ttl_exp |      0.006      0.013    0.469   0.639       -0.020       0.032
        _cons |     -1.761      0.719   -2.448   0.014       -3.171      -0.351
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The combined results are now the active estimates, so lincom, test, nlcom, and margins work on them, with each model’s coefficients referred to by the equation names shown in the output.

title: suest2
text:
Documentation
help suest2 in Stata documents the syntax and options. Examples of the full workflow are on the mecompare pages.
